content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed the magnitude attack and phase attack in the frequency domain and investigated the robustness of vision transformers under the proposed frequency domain attacks and regular pixel attacks, where the influence of image quality is controlled.  The image quality is measured by PSNR, MDSI, and LPIPS, and the authors mainly focused on PSNR. Under the same large PSNR (i.e., low quality), the authors showed that the relative robustness of vision transformers and CNNs could be different, where one important finding is that vision transformers are more vulnerable than CNNs under the phase attack when image quality is low.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength:**
+ The paper is overall well organized and presented. The experiments are well documented, and the authors tried to point out and discuss some of the unexpected results. 
+ The main finding that transformers are more vulnerable under certain conditions is interesting and consistent across different quality metrics. However, it would have been better if more details were clarified to support these findings. Please see the following weakness part:

**Weaknesses:**
- The necessity of using PSNR for image quality needs further clarification. Given the pairwise nature of PSNR, would $L_{2}$ norm of the perturbations already be a useful quality metric instead of PSNR? Accordingly, the findings could be formulated as the generated adversarial phase perturbations with a larger $L_{2}$ norm are more effective against transformers. The authors claimed in the introduction that attack strength (i.e.,  $L_{p}$) is not enough for evaluating the robustness of different models, however, PSNR is not a metric that is fundamentally different from the $L_{2}$. A clarification on this would be preferred.
- The image quality control could have been better motivated. Given the above concern of PSNR,  It's unclear why the image quality needs to be controlled to explore the model's robustness. The implication of the work needs to be further clarified.
- The PSNR control details are not discussed. If the PSNR is pre-defined before the perturbation generation, how is it controlled? If not, how are the images distributed regarding different PSNR values? For example, in Figure 1, are the ImageNet images perturbed to meet a pre-defined PSNR value, or are the perturbed images randomly distributed w.r.t different PSNR values? Given this concern, the experimental results are not very clear. If 95% of the perturbed images have a high quality, the results will be less influential. 
- In Fig. 1, the  PGD is only optimized with 50 steps. In contrast, the number of iterations for the proposed attack is 1000. Under white-box setups, as shown in [a],  would more optimization steps already be enough to increase the ASR to nearly 100% for all models? In addition, a comparison of the CW attack is preferred, since it controls $L_{2}$ norm (to some extent, equals to PSNR). It would be anticipated that the CW attack does not share the same results as FGSM and PGD, which means that conclusion that the robust difference between the transformers and CNNs may not hold.

**Minors:**
- In Figure 6, "whole" means that the attack leverages both low and high frequency. Given the right loss, it should automatically select the right one to perturb. How could this result of "whole" be worse than the other two when attacking ViT-B?
- Why perturbations for ResNet50 can be optimized more easily by the restriction?
- The description of Figure 4 mentioned that "the Transformers are similar to the ResNet models"
- An exploration of SSIM[b] would provide more evidence.

[a] On Adaptive Attacks to Adversarial Example Defenses. https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.08347

[b] Image Quality Assessment: From Error Visibility to Structural Similarity. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1284395
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The presentation is good, but some critical details (e.g., the PSNR control) could have been clarified further.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper investigates the robustness of vision transformers and CNNs by controlling the image quality, however, some critical contents, including details of quality control and the necessity of quality control, are not thoroughly discussed. In addition, the implication of the study is not clear. I would suggest rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In order to setup a uniform robust evaluation of both CNNs and Transformers, the paper suggests to consider image quality as an additional evaluation towards adversarial robustness. The paper proposes an attack, which perturbs magnitude, phase, and pixel of an image. Experiments show that Transformers rely more on phase information and low frequency information than CNNs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The idea of perturbing magnitude and phase is interesting. The designed attack is natural.
- This paper is well organized and clearly written, which allows an easy read.

Weakness:
- The motivation of considering image quality is based on unreliable attack strengths of FGSM and PGD. However, PGD attack may provide a false sense of robustness, that's why recent works consider stronger attack e.g., CW and AutoAttack. The authors are suggested to add these to as a solid evidence of current adv. attack is not reliable enough. 
- Moreover, besides adv. robustness, does certified robustness provide a better understanding of Transformers?
- How do you design eq(4)? How does it theoretically link to the attack? Is there any theoretically guarantee?
- For the experimental setup, models are pre-trained on different datasets which is not fair. I would suggest authors to both train and test on ImageNet-1k. WideResNet is suggested as well.
- For the evaluation, it is better to add adv. attacks (PGD, CW, AA) as a comparison with the designed attack.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper proposes an attack measuring image quality as an additional evaluation towards adversarial robustness.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper focuses on measuring image quality as another measure of robustness. I found the idea is natural. However, the experimental design is not fair and thorough, and it is lack of theoretical guarantee.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies the vulnerability of ViTs, in comparison to that of CNNs, to different types of adversarial attacks. To measure the strength of the attacks, possibly operating in different threat models, the paper proposes to use PSNR, which should approximate the perceptual similarity of the perturbed and original image. A framework for attacks in both pixel and spectral domain is then introduced: this allows to analyze how susceptible classifiers (on ImageNet) with various architectures are to several types of attacks and improve the understanding of the differences of the robustness of ViTs and CNNs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- Understanding the robustness of models with different architectures and which type of information they rely on for classification is a relevant topic. The insights provided by analyzing the effect of attacks operating in complementary threat models might be helpful in this direction.

- The framework to generate the attacks in both pixel and spectral (magnitude and phase) is a simple and reasonable way to obtain a variety of perturbation types.

Weaknesses
- Using PSNR to assess the strength of the attacks seems a bit problematic since it is not a metric the attacks optimize: for example, using an $\ell_\infty$-bounded attack and fixed a level of PSNR, there might be adversarial perturbations in the $\ell_\infty$-ball with the desired PSNR which are not found by PGD since they have lower loss values (the objective of the attack) than other points (similar arguments hold for other attacks). Then, it is not clear how to interpret a comparison based on PSNR.

- The paper compares the results of FGSM and PGD, but these operate in the same threat model, and the latter is just a stronger optimizer. Since robustness is evaluated in the worst-case scenario, it is unclear which insights the results of FGSM could add.

- It is observed that *"gradient-based attack methods tend to perturb high frequency features in images..."*, but I think this depends on the definition of the threat model (and maybe optimizer), e.g. using $\ell_2$- instead of $\ell_\infty$-constraints should yield lower frequency perturbations.

- It is hard to see the differences across threat models in Fig. 2.

- PGD with bound $\epsilon$ is used with $T$ iterations and step size $\epsilon/T$: this might be suboptimal (assuming that, as commonly done, the sign of the gradient is used) since with random start not every point in the feasible set can be reached.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Clarity: the presentation is overall clear (maybe a more formal introduction of the method in Sec. 3.2 could be given). The title suggests a focus on ViTs, but the evaluation reads more as a comparison between different versions of ViTs and CNNs.

- Quality: the approach of generating attacks in different domains is reasonable. However, the conclusions from the empirical evaluation rely on some unclear assumptions about the connections among threat models, optimizers, PSNR score and robustness of the classifiers (e.g. as mentioned above the PSNR score is not part of the objective function optimized by the attacks). This makes, in my opinion, the results somehow a bit hard to interpret.

- Novelty: previous works have proposed to generate perturbations in the Fourier space, and others have argued about the sensitivity of ViTs and CNNs to noise with various frequencies. The main novel aspects of the paper are, to my knowledge, the comprehensive analysis of the adversarial robustness to attacks generated in different domains and using PSNR as metric to determine the strength of an attack.

- Reproducibility: sufficient details are provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents some interesting results, especially the part about the sensitivity of ViTs and CNNs to attacks with various frequencies. However, I think there is some confusion about the connections among threat models, optimizers, PSNR score and robustness of the classifiers. Since the empirical evaluation is the main contribution of the paper, I think several points should be clarified to make it as interpretable and sound as possible.

content.title: Analyzing adversarial robustness of vision transformers against spatial and spectral attacks
content.abstract: Vision Transformers have emerged as a powerful architecture that can outperform convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in image classification tasks. Several attempts have been made to understand robustness of Transformers against adversarial attacks, but existing studies draw inconsistent results, i.e., some conclude that Transformers are more robust than CNNs, while some others find that they have similar degrees of robustness. In this paper, we address two issues unexplored in the existing studies examining adversarial robustness of Transformers. First, we argue that the image quality should be simultaneously considered in evaluating adversarial robustness. We find that the superiority of one architecture to another in terms of robustness can change depending on the attack strength expressed by the quality of the attacked images. Second, by noting that Transformers and CNNs rely on different types of information in images, we formulate an attack framework as a tool for implementing flexible attacks, where an image can be attacked in the spectral domain as well as in the spatial domain. This attack perturbs the magnitude and phase information of particular frequency components selectively. Through extensive experiments, we find that Transformers tend to rely more on phase information and low frequency information than CNNs, and thus sometimes they are even more vulnerable under frequency-selective attacks. It is our hope that this work provides new perspectives in understanding the properties and adversarial robustness of Transformers.
